title: Behavioral, mid product manager, strong answers, Example Corp values

questions.text: Tell me about a product you owned and a decision you would defend.
Tell me about a disagreement with engineering or design over scope.
Tell me about a launch that missed its goal.
Tell me about a time you explained a hard trade-off to executives.
Tell me about how you work with a team across several functions.
Tell me about a metric you moved and how.

probe_areas: Scope of ownership at current employer

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Hi Tomas, thanks for joining. I'm Hannah, a group product manager here. This is a forty-five minute behavioral conversation.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Hi Hannah, thanks for making the time.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How has your week been?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Good. We just closed a planning cycle, so it's a relief to have a quieter few days.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: I'll ask about four past experiences and probe where I'm curious. We'll keep time at the end for your questions.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a product you owned and a decision you would defend.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I owned the driver check-in flow at Brightwell Logistics for about two years. Drivers waited an average of 22 minutes at warehouse gates, so I led a redesign to a QR code check-in. I ran twelve driver interviews, wrote the spec, and decided to ship to three pilot sites first, even though sales wanted all forty at once. Gate wait dropped to 9 minutes in the pilot, and we rolled out to every site the next quarter.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Why pilot first instead of launching everywhere?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Two reasons. A bad check-in blocks trucks, so a bug was expensive, and I had no data on gates with poor mobile signal. The pilot showed that at two sites about 15 percent of drivers could not scan. I added a fallback code, which cost the engineers one extra week. That week was worth it. The full launch had a 98 percent success rate with scan or fallback.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a disagreement with engineering or design over scope.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: On that project, the lead engineer wanted to cut offline mode to hit the date. I thought offline was the core need because gates often have weak signal. I did not argue opinions. I pulled gate logs showing 31 percent of check-ins happened on weak signal, and I offered to cut the admin dashboard instead. He agreed, because the dashboard could use existing reports. We shipped on the original date with offline mode, and the dashboard followed six weeks later.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a launch that missed its goal.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I launched text reminders for delivery appointments with a goal of cutting missed appointments by 20 percent. After six weeks the drop was only 4 percent. I had assumed drivers forgot, but I had not checked. I owned the miss in our review and then called 15 drivers. Most missed because of traffic or gate delays, not forgetting.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What did you change after that?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I changed the reminder to include a live arrival estimate and an easy reschedule link. I also set a rule for my team: no launch goal without five customer calls first. The next version cut missed appointments by 17 percent in two months, and the rule is now in our planning template.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a time you explained a hard trade-off to executives.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Last year the CFO asked me to cut the roadmap by a third. I built a one page view with each item's cost, expected revenue and risk, and I proposed dropping three low-return items to protect the gate project. I told them plainly that this delayed two sales requests by a quarter. I also walked the sales head through the reasons before the meeting, so she was not surprised. The CFO approved it in one meeting, and we kept 90 percent of the planned revenue impact.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Thanks, that's helpful. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: How does your team decide what to say no to each quarter?

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: We rank by expected impact and cost, then review with engineering leads, and about a third of requests are declined with a written reason.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: That's our time. Thanks Tomas, the recruiter will follow up within a week.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Thank you, Hannah. I enjoyed it.

notes: Strong for mid: own role, numbers and trade-offs in every answer.
